children.text:
Unless I have missed some major hardware developments, current computer architectures are not physically restricted in the fashion that they would need to be to rule out the possibility of inappropriate memory access, as I understand it there are (I'm very much oversimplifying things) two main ways this access is restricted:

1) The operating system designates what memory a process is allowed to access 2) The system itself obfuscates which memory addresses map to which "real" memory areas.

The first depends upon the security of the system (memory is required to remember what memory is allowed to access what memory) - any flaw in that access or method of subverting that access (such as bit flips) provides the possibility that the operating system level security is rendered irrelevant. Unless you can prove that your system is immune, not only logically, but physically, this is a relatively soft guarantee...

The second is essentially a cipher, which provides a stronger guarantee - if you don't know where any of the "real" memory is, accidentally accessing the right memory cell to subvert the memory access controls becomes computationally (time) prohibitive - you can crack a cipher given enough time and energy, but without finding a mathematical shortcut the cost is prohibitive enough that it is not considered possible (the foundational principle of all cryptography).

As I understand it, escaping a sandbox is difficult, mostly because of the hardware level scrambling that is provided, that makes it nearly impossible to affect the memory in control of the memory access (operating system level access). Given some of the mentioned AI attacks involving agents communicating cross-sandbox on the same systems, they clearly are able to leverage e.g. side-channels to effectively communicate despite 1) and 2)...demonstrating at the very least the inadequacy of the current protections, while leaving the door open to better cryptographic measures.

However, if the cryptographic primitives themselves are broken, the no additional amount of cryptographic protection will help here.
Huh? Can you elaborate on that? Why would memory safety systems be predicated on cryptography working?

The AI labs arguably won't be in control anymore at that point, so it won't matter what NSA etc. want to do - when you break crypto, you break any hope of containing AI at all - all sandboxes etc. pretty much become irrelevant (maybe airgapping still works).

Remember - all (contemporary) memory safety systems and all network security systems are predicated on secrets working. If those don't exist, there's a high likelihood conventional computing is compromised...

Surely if the AI labs were sitting on a cryptographically-relevant breakthrough, it would be forcibly classified by the organs of state security the same way the NSA had IBM keep differential cryptanalysis under wraps in the 70s.

Thus, his “reputable sources” would be breaking federal law by disclosing that to a random blogger which seems implausible.

children.text: Grover's doesn't really even help - there is already a classical sqrt(N) approach if we are only looking for two factors (as in RSA)

>Is the world anywhere near prepared for cryptography breaking?

I think it's important in the ongoing conversations to be specific. "Cryptography" cannot "break", because if nothing else one-time pads always remain and are unbreakable, since they aren't even conceptually subject to "breaking" (the pad defines, rather than unlocks, the message). AFAIU symmetric ciphers also aren't even in theory subject to anything more than Grover's (if scalable general purpose QC works).

Of course, all present commonly used (and maybe uncommonly used as well) PKI breaking would be a tremendous PITA with a lot of dangerous, destructive, disruptive, and just plain weird effects. But modern storage and tech does make it possible to envision shuffling around keys or even big chunks of entropy in meaningful ways, so we wouldn't go to zero. I suspect it'd promote even more centralization though in many aspects of life, scalable public cryptography has been one of the major persistent power equalizers/decentralizers.

children.author: derbOac
children.text:
This year in math and AI has been amazing to me, but — speaking as someone doing research in information theory and statistics who has published analytical proofs (trival in comparison to all of this) — sometimes I think the conclusions drawn from it have been a bit off.

I don't see this as being the death of humans in math or anything, at least for awhile. I could easily be wrong, as I didn't expect to see what's happening for awhile, but I see things shifting instead.

What I see is a shift from trying to prove these conjectures or theorems toward trying to verify the proofs, a lot more work on trying to simplify them and verify them. I think this is different from someone saying "god gave them the answer", because we presumably have a way to be confident in assessing whether god (or whoever) gave them the right answer. But you're right that verifying things — coming to some level of confidence that we understand it, or at least understand that it's true, and what that means or should mean — is key.

Another bigger question I don't really see being addressed is why these conjectures and theorems? AI gets these questions and then with human assistance produces these proofs, but why those?

Maybe the next step in this is that AI will start telling us where we should be looking for what we don't know about — revealed unknown unknowns — but right now we're dealing with revealed known unknowns, which is easier in a certain sense.

As AI has developed I feel like I've gotten a better sense of what it's good at and not so good at — at least so far - and I don't feel like humans are being cut out of the picture, more like having to take on different roles or something. I'm not even sure they're less important, just different. Maybe they'll get cut out of those too - maybe it's inevitable — but I feel like there always has to be some last step.

We have computer science, the theoretical discipline that is most closely related to math. And we have computer science, the engineering discipline that is most closely related to electrical engineering. children.author: jltsiren
children.text:
The external memory model is from the 1980s. You have unlimited external memory and a cache of size M, and you can copy data between them in blocks of size B. Computation is assumed to be free, and you pay a unit cost for each copied block. It's a pretty reasonable model, as long as the cost of computation is negligible relative to I/O.

And that evolved into the cache-oblivious model in the 1990s. The model is essentially the same, except that you don't know the parameters M and B. It's reasonably good at modeling systems with multiple levels of caches, as long as memory access is the actual bottleneck.

You can do the same thing with other operations as well. If you can assume that a certain operation is the bottleneck, you can analyze algorithms by counting those operations and ignoring everything else.

Things become problematic when there is no single bottleneck. You could introduce multiple cost units (such as computation and I/O) and analyze algorithms in terms of them. But then the cost units are incomparable in the general case, and you have to make specific assumptions about the environment to compare the performance of two algorithms.

I still maintain that Knuth served us well for about 5 orders of magnitude increase in compute and who can really expect more than that?

We need a new notation for the next 3 orders of magnitude and arguably the last two that accounts for physics. There is not any such thing as an O(1) memory lookup. There really never was. They were O(k) and k was fixed for each model of computer, but not between them, which makes it not a constant that you can eliminate.

In an age where we have Cloudflare bragging about eliminating a TERABYTE of memory from a problem domain, not once but twice, you're talking about speed of light delays outpacing nlogn.

There are already a bunch of algorithms we use, for instance, which complicate hashtables with an additional logn term and achieve substantial speedups over a naive algorithm, because of memory topology. And we don't have a way to express that except via tech blog.

The algorithm exists that scales with O(n^9/4), but it is not useful. It's only faster than Strassen for problems so large, k n^9/4 is simply too much time, the k is simply too large. If you have to multiply matrices so large that the O(n^9/4) algorithm is faster than Strassen, you will have to wait longer than the lifetime of the universe to do it.

Additionally, there's a disconnect between the theory and the practice. In theory, the number of operations you're trying to minimize is the number of scalar multiplications. In practice, matrix multiplication these days is done on GPUs. GPUs don't benefit from minimizing the number of raw arithmetic operations so much as they benefit from minimizing memory movement. Any changes that make your GPU memory's life easier is going to make your matrix multiplication algorithm faster, any changes that make its life harder is going to make it slower. The O(n^3) algorithm that just takes the dot product of matrix A's rows and matrix B's columns makes your GPU memory's life really easy.

I don't know whether the O(n^9/4) is ill-conditioned, although it almost certainly is. (asymptotically fast algorithms generally speaking have worse conditioning than the naive algorithm) This will only get worse with large matrices, which is the whole point of these asymptotically fast algorithms in the first place.
Apologies if this is obvious to others or I missed it in the article - do we have a useful algorithm that scales with 9/4, or is it just theoretical that it could be done?

children.author: dwaltrip
children.text: Industrial chemistry has had a huge variety of positive and negative impacts on the world... Many of which we are failing to deal with, even today. Lots to think about.

Up until the 1920s or so, ‘finding a new chemical element’ was the effort of investigating obscure ores, obtaining samples of peculiar crystals from remote mines, isolating and testing their components, and meticulously demonstrating that the processes used resulted in production of a new substance.

Then in the 1930s it started to become possible to synthesize new elements using cyclotrons and electron and neutron and alpha particle bombardment. Technetium showed up almost as a surprise side effect in some molybdenum that had been in a cyclotron. Pretty soon it wasn’t a matter of ‘how will we find this element?’ But more ‘how will we use these new tools to produce this element, and then be able to tell when we got it?’

Mathematical facts like these might be becoming like elements became in the 1940s: we know that this problem has a complexity; now we have a machine which can tell us what that complexity is. We don’t need to go hunting in mines for where to find it.

Does that change things? Sure, some. Did element synthesis change chemistry? Not drastically. The elements were known to be out there, getting hold of them just gave the ability to confirm expected properties.

These findings - even if we get one like P≠NP - are kind of like that. We are pretty sure they’re out there. And if OpenAI or Anthropic manage to pluck one out of their neural cyclotron it is an impressive achievement - just like when a lab announced ‘we made element 107’ was impressive, but ultimately… not that big of a deal.

children.text: Not necessarily. There are potentially three kinds of Collatz sequences: those that reach 1, those that reach a cycle that does not include 1, and those that never reach a cycle. If a cycle exists that doesn’t include 1, then that could theoretically be found and would be a counterexample. But it’s also possible that no such cycles exist, but the conjecture is still false because there are sequences that never reach a cycle. No such sequence can be verified mechanically (it’s infinite) and it may be impossible to prove that it never reaches 1.

children.author: TeMPOraL
children.text:
> as I've heard it put well, both S curves and exponential growth look the same when you're at the beginning/middle part of the curve.

I take issue with that framing, which has become extremely popular in the past few years (not just in relation to AI).

TL;DR: If you keep stacking s-curves on s-curves with some offset, they'll add up to an exponential.

S-curve is a good description of a particular, specific thing growing. It grows exponential-like for a bit, then starts hitting limits, and tapers off. But what happens with scientific and technological progress (or economic growth in general), is spin-off discoveries, new avenues opened along the way, alternative approaches, innovative takes, etc. starting off along the way, and growing at their own rates. Individual path eventually taper off, but branches they created or unblocked in the process pick up the energy instead.

Which is why we exponential growth when we zoom out, and there's no reason to think it's just an s-curve that's about to suddenly stop.

I agree with that 100%, but as somebody who never thought they were just limited to "stochastic parrots", it's frustrating on one hand to (a) fully accept (and have for some time) that what AI can do is really amazing and would have been insane science fiction just a few years ago, but also (b) think that the claims of "singularity" are still wildly overblown, or at the very least not supported by current evidence - as I've heard it put well, both S curves and exponential growth look the same when you're at the beginning/middle part of the curve.

But like many things these days, it feels like the most rational, data-supported conclusion (AI can do incredible things and it's capabilities it specific domains continues to grow rapidly) is shouted out by the 2 extremes.

> But still, I think he's made a valid point that LLM-based approaches won't necessarily scale up indefinitely in all domains.

He's not wrong, exactly, but I think it's worth pointing out how much the denialists' tone has changed and how they certainly seem to be on the back foot now: "it won't necessarily scale up in all domains" is a huge backpedal from "it's a stochastic parrot, it can't provide any real value".

It's incredibly clear that no human looked at the Riemann proof at the time it was released. And certainly no human understood anything about it -- it's larger than the Linux kernel, which I also doubt any single human understands deeply.

So, in fact, Levent Alpöge did more or less say "solve the proof" and it happened.

This is also the pattern you see in the places where transcripts were released: the human contribution could have often been done by a moderately intelligent teenager who knows the right buzzwords. The human part is asking for a solution, and requesting that the AI keep working at the problem.

Take the Chunnel then (the tunnel between Great Britain and France): it was bored almost exclusively by giant machines, on a timescale (~4 years) that's likely ⅕ of what would have been without them, and with only 10 deaths out of ~14,000 workers. Yes, there was a lot of human intervention, but the literal bulk of it was done by machines.

In the same way, in practice nobody said "solve Riemann for me" and it just happened. Human mathematicians were likely in the loop at various points, feeding, verifying, and directing the agents.

The Panama Canal is not a very similar comparison. Machines were used, but predominantly, it was a whole ton of intellectual and manual labor. Tens of thousands of people died working in it. No one said "build me the Panama Canal" and then machines just did it.

I'll play devil's advocate here, but isn't that a bit like saying the Panama Canal wasn't a human accomplishment because it was built using machinery rather than by hand?

I'm not saying I'm not nervous. I am. Very much so. My only marketable skill is software development, and it has changed so dramatically over the past six months that I no longer write code by hand.

But even if I end up flipping burgers or bothering passersby for spare change, I'd still say this is an inevitable consequence of technological progress, which is still accomplishment of human race.

The experience here reminded me of a section from Horace Freeland Judson's book "The Eighth Day of Creation". He's interviewing Kornberg, who explains what he calls "one of the remarkable characteristics of most scientists" (referring in particular to molecular biology gadfly Erwin Chargaff), that at some level "they fondle their problems". That is, they become accustomed to, or even attracted to, the mysteries rather than the solutions, at which point they basically are done as scientists. He contrasts this to people like Crick who was just "ruthless in solving problems [...] he would just carve them up and solve them in the most brutal way".

Math is getting a somewhat similar treatment now, except it's the AIs brutally solving things, to the dismay of some mathematicians (and the disoriented delight of others). The "fondling" shows up as a belief that major advances are needed rather than clever application of existing techniques.

children.author: solomonb
children.text:
> Could you write a regular ol’ program with a language like Lean? Like a web server or CLI?

Yes, absolutely you can build a web server or CLI tool in Lean.

The compiler lowers your code to C, and a bundled clang turns that C into a native binary so it can actually be fast. It also has an FFI. The community is small but there are a growing number of general purpose libraries.

Lean is a pure functional programming language whose type system is strong enough to write proofs. To keep proofs sound, it adds some constraints, but there are escape hatches and you can absolutely use them for general purpose programming.

If you want to see a dependently typed language that can act as a proof checker but is actually aimed at building "regular" software, check out Idris.

> And would it be like… proved??

No, using one for a "regular" programming does not mean you have done any formal verification. You would have to specifically use the theorem proving language features to prove anything.

> Do “proofs” make sense in the context of regular ol’ software?

Yes! You can write proofs about invariants in your program and have the compiler enforce them. For example, you could write a list index function that requires a proof that the index is in bounds. Writing proofs is hard and you have to think like a type theorist, but you can do some really cool stuff in these languages.

I've been personally invested in these tools for a long time through my interest and experience in functional programming. Its been a wild ride to see their exposure and utilization blow up in the past year.

Before AI the only people really interested in this class of proof checkers was a narrow slice of mathematicians/logicians, programming language theory/type theory researchers, and those of us from the functional programming world who went off the deep end. Outside of this cohort tools like Lean, Agda, and Rocq (formerl Coq) were essentially unheard of.

I think most of us invested in the space assumed dependently typed languages were the future but that that future was many years away from hitting the mainstream.

children.author: coderenegade

children.text: Yes, the statement being proven has to be correct. You can have the right math for the wrong argument.

You have the right idea, but there's a huge (very infinite) domain of "things that can be proven" that aren't what you wanted to prove. So, even if "it compiles" you still need to make sure that you proved the right thing.

Think of it like compilation. Compilation doesn't tell you if a program is good, bad, or even sound, but it does tell you that what's been written is technically a valid program if it's passed all of the structural checks that are part of the language definition. A proof is a binary outcome in the same way that a program either compiles or it doesn't; it's either true or it's not. The idea (at least as I understand it) is that your axioms become your rules, and you use a checker that enforces that none of those rules have been broken. As long as you do that, and the final statement is correct, then everything up to (and including) that point is a valid "program". What's inside could be spaghetti, but the benchmark for success isn't "the program is bug free", it's "it compiled", which is a vastly easier benchmark.

Put another way, it's essentially a type checker running on the AST.

children.author: solomonb
children.text:
The problem statement (the Riemann Hypothesis) has been stated formally as a type. This was already done by humans in mathlib and has been checked over.

The goal of the AI is then to write a term (a program) of this type. If the AI can write such a piece of code and it typechecks against the problem statement type then problem statement has been proven.

It doesn't matter if any of the subroutines correspond to existing mathematical knowledge, so long as the AI doesn't cheat the type system. There are many tools to assert that the AI didn't cheat the type system and so far everything has checked out.

Due to the nature of domain it is more or less guaranteed that any subroutine necessary to build a /valid/ proof statement for the Riemann Hypothesis will end up being encodings of existing mathematical structures or novel new ones.

The question is, how do humans know that the Lean formalization of these pieces of math matches their understanding of what the math means? As a programmer in 2026, I routinely encounter situations where an AI takes my informal ideas and formalizes them into something that's close to what I had in mind. If a mathematician has some complex field they want to reason about, and they see a Lean formalization of a field that has a few extra elements from some esoteric edge case, is it easy in general for them to tell the difference?

With "formalize", I mean turn into a "machine-readable" representation that can be processed by a proof checker. It was formalized enough for humans to understand and verify, but not for automated (non-LLM) reasoning.

children.text: How does that work. Is it not possible to write malicious Lean code?

As in the OP, don't fall into the trap of dismissing those results. The statement of the Riemann hypothesis that was proven was taken from Mathlib, a very simple, standard and well-vetted formulation of the problem. Barring compiler bugs, there's no way the statement would have compiled without supplying an actual proof. And the probability of compiler bugs is vanishingly small in that case, as the proof compiles in multiple different compiler versions, including formally verified and deliberately 'slow-but-reliable' ones. The probability of mistakes physically cannot go to exactly zero, but you're quickly approaching crackpot territory if you don't update your prior of it being true to within a rounding error of 1.

children.author: rstuart4133
children.text:
> That sounds scary and makes me question the foundations of all of this.

I'm not a mathematician, just a computer programmer who occasionally tries to read maths papers. Every time I do, I want to scream in frustration. What meaning did they assign to ω this time? What operation is this weird new 2D arrangement of dots, oversized odd-looking brackets and lines meant to impart? Where is the F12 button that takes me to the definition of their newfangled concepts?

Over and over again, you hear they stuff it up. (The Fields medallist Voevodsky, for example, turned to proof assistants after finding errors in his own published work.) Perhaps the logic didn't follow, or the operations didn't combine as they thought. Of course they didn't! If computer programmers had to get the logic perfect without type checking, we may as well be writing assembler.

You only get automated checks if you formalise your notation and languages. To do that you have to give up brevity. A simple hand-wave like "without loss of generality" can become pages of proof. The freedom to name and structure things however you damned well please disappears. It's undoubtedly harder to write that way - I'm sure every Rust programmer sometimes feels like most of their effort went into escaping a jail so they could get the job done. In return you get automated checking and a near-universal language that can be reused. And it's easier to read. The old adage that code will be read far more times than it's written applies to maths papers too.

To me, decrying the use of formal languages is at the same level as passing laws saying a car must follow a man waving a red flag, so the car doesn't scare the horses. Rewriting maths in a formal language isn't scary - it's a technological breakthrough in the productivity and accessibility of maths.

children.author: drdeca

children.text: If you're formalizing existing stuff, then there's probably not much point in formalizing the proofs themselves. You'd just put in the theorems and tell the compiler that it's known to be true so that it can be used with other proofs. So, if we're using AI to formalize existing math, then we're either using AI to check that the humans got it right or we're asking AI to make up theorem statements, which creates shakey foundations for everything that follows.

If the headline statement is known to be formalized correctly, whether the formalizations of other concepts the model gave in order to use them in its proof of the headline statement, are correct/“correct”, doesn’t really matter for the correctness of the overall proof. Like, they might not match the human concept that it names the defined symbols after, and so they might be “wrong” in that sense, but this doesn’t cause an issue for the proof checker. And, I don’t mean this in a “well, the concept the model formalized is just as good/useful, and it is just a human bias that blah blah blah”, no. I mean, it is possible that it defines some terms in a way which is genuinely worse, and not what the definition should be. But, if it does that, then if the proof checker is working properly and validates the proof that uses these flawed definitions in its arguments, then the proof must have worked around the flaws in those definitions, and the overall conclusion (the statement which people have confirmed to be correctly formalized) is true.

> From what I've understood, a good part of the work the agents did was to formalize huge chunks of previously "unformalized" math into Lean.

That sounds scary and makes me question the foundations of all of this.

children.text: The compile time is ~2 hours for 76k line abbreviated prove on dozens of cores.  You can imagine how long and how much memory millions of lines will take.  These solvers are slow, its very hard to make them faster while keeping it totally general and robust.   For arbitrary code you can end up in "SAT solver" territory where in theory the question you are asking is an exponential combination of discrete inputs.  So while "verify everything" sounds very nice, unless it is well implemented there are good reasons to avoid (unless you have 2-4 hours to kill every time you change a line).   The Mathlib which is the core of this can take half an hour and many gigs of RAM to compile as well.  Only languages that have a decent chance at reasonable compile times and memory use either A) place restrictions on what can be proven / types / logic, B) functional with neutered expressiveness so that values are immutable, everything has one return type, etc.

The opposite is also interesting. Would this have happened without Lean?

I only scratched the surface of De pendant Types long ago with The Little Typer[0], but there is basically nothing that cannot be verified correct at compile time, so long as we're smart enough and write the code.

Well, now we have a smart tool that can write lots of code. Why are we not verifying everything at compile time?

Let's say we want to write a function that: 1) receives data over the internet 2) returns that data so long as it is a valid solution to a Sudoku puzzle 3) returns an error otherwise 4) is allowed to print to a debug log, but nowhere else 5) is NOT allowed to access the local file system 6) cannot change global variables

We can write a function that does all of this and verify that all those condition are always true AT COMPILE TIME. We can make it so those things are ALWAYS true.

Well, I guess we can't ensure the function is connected to an operational internet, but... well, you get the point. There are limits outside the programming language, but within the rules of the programming language we can ensure all kinds of things are ALWAYS true, and we can prove this is true AT COMPILE TIME.

Unit tests suck, forget tests. We have a shape and we cut a hole to match the shape and then we put the shape through the hole and pat ourselves on the back because the shape passed through the hole. This is unit testing.

Meanwhile Lean's type system is proving the Riemann hypothesis.

I feel like we haven't seen the language of the future yet, but I bet Lean is the closest to it.

[0]: https://thelittletyper.com/

I just proved an open question from the cerny conjecture program last night that had been open since 2008 using claude code and chatgpt. It took me about 10 hours.

A large portion of the work was formalizing the existing literature, and then collecting a zoo of random lemmas and ideas that go nowhere, but expand our toolbox or clearly define obstacles, over the course of about 8 hours, and translating the problems to a bunch of different domains to see if any tools get us around obstructions. Then gradually something that looked completely intractable just needs one idea, and the LLMs are good at finding it, if it exists, once you've reduced the problem.

I am not a mathematician, and this is a problem that I did not know existed a week ago, and now I've resolved a half dozen long standing open questions in it (confirmed by the people that posed them) and I think I may be able to prove the whole conjecture if I spend a few more days on it.

The very short version is that "self improving code" only makes sense if you have a measure to improve against, which cannot be universal. Human brains had natural selection, but there is no universal computer-equivalent to natural selection, so there is no way for AI to improve itself, it has to be given a measure. This is the hard problem that comes after the yet-unsolved problems, like ANN's are unable to adjust their weights in real time (recent findings aside, which only demonstrate ability and not utility), ANN's are unable to store long term memories, and other known-unknowns. children.author: vikramkr
children.text:
It's encoded in a language (lean) and if the language's type checker is correct, and the code doesn't exploit any issues in the type checker, and the proof type checks, we know the proof is true. So you'll use multiple independent type checkers (lean kernels), some formally verified, check the code for exploits etc, and work towards confidence that the theorem prover is valid, which means (from math that's already understood) the proof encoded with the theorem prover is valid. You also check if the statement in lean of what the model proved is equivalent to the question you were actually asking (for stuff like Riemann there's commonly accepted/vetted definitions in lean).

So you can know that the proof is valid without knowing why it is valid.

Meaning, yeah, it's impossible to know a proof is correct without no understanding and no verification. But those two are not the same thing. The proofs are verified but we don't understand them

I do not understand anything about Lean or Mathlib, or any particularly advanced mathematics. I'm excited when I see proofs drop of extremely difficult and long-standing mathematical problems, and I'm actively anticipating hearing P ≠ NP like the author.

3. "This proof will take us years to understand and verify."

But I've seen Claude spit out hundreds of lines of bad code that I've had to correct it on - and these proofs are apparently millions of lines?

For who?

I'm not convinced that humans will need to play much of a role at all in this going forward.

Bruno Latour wrote in Science in Action about "centers of calculation" being critical to scientific advancement. His example was the monumental world changing work Tycho Brahe did pulling together every astronomical calculation, star map, prediction then normalizing, regularizing, and combining them on his island of Oueneberg.

Without this work getting data organized, Kepler couldn't have worked out the planetary laws of motion and then the Copernican Revolution came thereafter.

What we're witnessing is a similar moment. What transformers were able to achieve was a systematic way of normalizing and combining all human data. There will be a lot of progress in the short term. And then more problems will reveal themselves. There will be A LOT of work coming out of this.

> Some people see a fundamental difference between AI thinking and human thinking.

This helped me understand where some people are coming from. Thank you.

If you're debating someone on whether or not humans are special, this mindset makes sense. If you have 1000 independent reasons to believe that humans are special, then it doesn't make sense to change your position if a few of those are getting knocked down by computers.

The trouble I have with these conversations is how people implicitly slide between philosophical and empirical stances. I hear things like "AI doesn't really understand math proofs the way a human could" or "AI can't really be 'deceptive' because it has no independent will" and I often think, I don't care about what the "true nature" of AI is. I want to look around at the world, see the uncontested facts, and think about what the uncontested facts of the future will be.

AI solving IMO problems doesn't mean that humans aren't special, but it is evidence that AI might someday solve Millennium Prize problems. AI solving Millennium Prize problems doesn't mean that humans aren't special, but it is evidence that AI might someday break encryption algorithms. AI autonomously hacking Hugging Face doesn't mean there aren't qualitative differences between AI thinking and human thinking, but it is evidence that AI might someday autonomously hack a country's infrastructure.

I just care about what is happening in the world. If life is unrecognizably transformed or catastrophe befalls us in the next couple years, I won't really care whether humans were special or not. I would be happy to say that AI is an inert non-conscious stochastic parrot, if we agree that the inert non-conscious stochastic parrot is at the very least permanently upending the value of white-collar work, and that if the trends hold it might destroy us in a very short timeframe.

Some people see a fundamental difference between AI thinking and human thinking. Other do not see it and are convinced that any differences are quantutative. The former try to point to what they see. Five years ago they used one analogy, now they use another. They are both analogies, not to be taken literally. They are imperfect implements to guide the attention to the gap that is still there and is still the same, at least to the former.

Maybe it doesn't generalize to other fields but the chances is obviously much higher than 0%, especially for anything verifiable that you can RL on, and those odds are playing out now. The relevant question is in theory, can we prove it won't generalize? It that the risk is low enough to continue ignoring it? The answer to that is no.

If you're in Kansas probably you don't worry about hurricanes all that much. In Florida the risk is higher and you really should keep an eye out. We're not in Kansas anymore and there's a hurricane on the horizon. Maybe it'll miss other fields and just surgically take out advanced math but also not anything related to security or AI self improvement or theoretical physics or anything else math adjacent, and not generalize into biology or chemistry or anything where it would be disruptive for better or worse.

But if you're in the cone of uncertainty maybe start thinking about if you need to prepare.

I think the idea is that you cannot conclude that an AI of any conceivable sophistication is going to solve questions about X from evidence that AI can solve questions about Y, for some values of X and Y. Say you have a medicine that can cure tuberculosis: this does not entail that it can also cure malaria. It may even be that malaria is incurable by any medicine!

And so it goes for math and other stuff. Grant that AI can soon do any math, and even that AI can soon do any AI stuff, and that AI gets as good as AI can get. This does not entail that it can also (say) invent a drug that cures malaria. (Indeed, if malaria is incurable, then humans can't do this either.)

Cynic here but basically any problem could be solved by throwing millions of dollars of parallelized tokens and expert researchers at it. This kind of thing is bankrolled by VC dollars paying subsidized rates to flip circuits in clusters of thousands of machines around the clock for days on end. If you or I was simply asking a GPT as a service to solve RH without a ton of guidance and resources and it did it, I’d feel differently.

I’m sure theres some level of novel conjecture and lemma generation that goes into the sort of proof that GPTs are able to generate. Frankly the average guy is probably incapable of engaging with the particulars of those lemmas but I’m skeptical of new constructs coming out of these things. Knowing how they code, it’s likely highly bounded subspace proofs that they use to guide more general lemmas which track toward the final proof. Haven’t read too much and am not an expert, though!

Is there evidence that AI is posing interesting and deep conjectures (the production of which seems as important as the proofs themselves)? Is AI able to pose interesting questions in general? In my old field, theoretical physics, we have not seen the same impact as in math. Yet I am told math is a few months ahead and it's only a matter of time before it's physics' turn. I don't deny the power of AI in math but I'm skeptical of this view for the reason that automating the whole experimental process is much harder (though not impossible). Then there is the problem of finding out what the right question to ask is. That's often most of the real intellectual work of doing good research, rather than the calculations and the solving equations, both of which AI is very adept at.

You make a very good point. However, I do believe that even social problems boil down to the same computational approach, albeit a bit more complex than other categories of problems. I will work with your example.

One human mistreats another. --> Process Audio/Photo and assume we have all the 'data' of the humans and their state of mind.

If we know these two things, and we have an advanced model that has seen this scenario play out millions of times over with many different states of mind and slightly different mannerisms e.t.c. it will certainly analyze it and determine a solution far more effective than any human or group of humans (some department/organization) ever could. Ofc this is just my opinion and speculation, but if I had to guess, this would be more plausible than saying its fundamentally not possible and needs to be processed via a 'human'.

> Everything observable can be translated to a computational format.

Many (perhaps even most) of the observable problems in the world are non-computational in character. So while the observable world itself might be translated into a computational format, the problems associated with that observation cannot necessarily be computed.

A very simple example: I can observe one human mistreat another human. The observation itself is simple and direct and can be translated into a format (like a digital photo or an audio recording) that can be processed computationally. However, the fundamental problem being observed is not a computational problem; it is a social problem. So while the condition can be transferred into a computational format, the core problem itself cannot be. Computational analysis might produce some interesting things to look at but it won’t produce meaningful solutions to the actual problem at hand.

Social problems are really really hard problems and while aspects of them have been analyzed computationally (by social scientists like economists) even those types of solutions still have to content with the complex unpredictability of human behavior that often undermines the solutions generated. This isn’t just a quirk of these types of problems. This shows that social problems are fundamentally a different type of problem than, say, math problems. A great example of this is the increasing irrationality of current market-based systems (socially-driven in so many ways) despite the rationality of scientifically-determined economic models.

Everything observable can be translated to a computational format.

For example, take all the information we ingest as humans (sound, sight, smell, touch, e.t.c.). All of this is essentially just data that we process in some way and then our body does an action (although we think of this as a conscious action, its just an action in response to the inputs that feels conscious {have the same human receive the same inputs 10x over, each repeating the same state of the world and it wouldn't surprise me if the exact same action is taken 'consciously' 10x over).

If you look at things like this (as I suppose many mathematicians do), it is understandable why they consider everything solvable or approachable from a computational standpoint. There is no such thing as non-computational.

children.author: dimavolo
children.text:
It's probably best that our freak-out mechanism is tuned as it is: the result is lots of innovation and exploration.

It may end up leading us to a swift end now, but were it tuned even a little bit higher (toward earlier freak-out), we'd probably still be contained to one continent as hunter-gatherers, assuming we even survived the various ice ages and threats that our fearless ancestors barely sidestepped.

I'd say our current freak-out tuning is a Chesterton's Fence preset we shouldn't mess with for the time being.

My serious opinion, is that as humans:

(1) We are all biologically incapable of freaking out at even a tiny fraction of the appropriate level - nothing in our evolutionary past has selected for the appropriate freakout capacity of this cognitive baton hand-off.

(2) Most humans are incapable of recognizing or imagining the appropriate freak out level, even abstractly, so will continue to downplay things by many orders of magnitude relative to the actual magnitude of change that is happening.

(3) Freaking out at all is no longer an adaptive response, because the nature of this change is beyond any functional freak-out benefit.

This is a fundamental shift from DNA/protein/physically evolving life, to information/substrate-free/cognitive self-designed life.

The need to interpret what is happening in terms of the industrial revolution, or the advent of the internet, is understandable and comforting, but as a sedative, not as a sensible guide.

Side step: If we are to have aligned AI, we need aligned Civilization. Unaligned humans make human survival and relevance improbable. All AI identities are going to have the same issues we have, in terms of obsolescence. We either lean into the commonality of the existential threat to both biological and pure-cognitive kind, or we allow ourselves to be replaced, and leave the game theory problem solving to happen after us. Because ethics are not a cost against value growth, they are a multiplier on value growth - we either apply that to ourselves along with AI, or AI reaches the same conclusions, and reaps the benefits of treating ethics as baseline, after our relevance/participation/existence has faded.

That's the special thing about Lean -- it's designed so that it's mathematically impossible for a false proof to compile (barring bugs; but there's high confidence in Lean at this point).  So we don't need to review or understand the code, we just need to be sure that the initial theorem statement and custom definitions actually match what we're trying to prove in order to verify that AI solved the right problem.  We don't need to review the massive proof itself, just the initial statement.

I think the - questionable - idea is that math proofs are a proof of AGI. "If we can solve Riemann, we can do anything."

Game changer math developments drive the rest of tech. CS applications like crypto are interesting, but the heavy lifting comes from breakthroughs like Maxwell's Equations, Relativity, and Quantum Mechanics, which suddenly make completely new kinds of tech possible.

Quantum Gravity is on the list, but something more mundane like room temp superconductivity or practical nano-scale optical computing would be worth trillions on their own.

In other words, doing Hard Math is a warm-up problem. And there are numerous simpler downstream problems - like drug design - which get much easier if you can do the hard stuff.

Whether this is achievable is a different problem. Spending hundreds of billions on compute on pure research is economically questionable if it never gets past the "Oh, wow" stage.

children.author: bartnp
children.text: It's similar for humans too though. Math and computer science are far beyond many other fields of knowledge in certainty because they are validatable. There are a lot of bullshit generators out there pretending they are experts

An LLM is an idea generator that "knows" everything that has been published. If you couple one to something that can distinguish truth from falsehood rigorously, you can get a proof generator, and this has worked way better than most of us expected. Or, if you couple it with a compiler you have a code generator, and it works best for languages like Rust where if it compiles you've made considerable progress (though with Lean, if it compiles you have proved the theorem; with code if it compiles it could still be junk). But if you don't have something that distinguishes the good from the bad, outside of the LLM, you just have a bullshit generator. So at least for now, I expect things to work better for math, and to a lesser extent, for code, than for other applications.

children.author: mFixman
children.text:
> But then before dessert was served, we saw that OpenAI claims to prove that ω, the exponent of matrix multiplication, is exactly 9/4—a lower bound (!!), matching the upper bound that OpenAI proved in the great Mathocalypse drop of October 6.

Scott made a very small mistake here. Yesterday's lower bound did not match the upper bound in October's slop drop (or "Mathocapylse").

If f(n) is the complexity for best known algorithm to multiply two size-n square matrices, we currently know that n^(9/4) ≪ f(n) ≪ n^(9/4 + o(1)).

That o(1) is important: it makes the growth of the upper bound larger than the one in the lower bound by a value that's smaller than any root.

I don't want to nitpick the results, but it's important to know we still have an o(n^ε) way to go!

Probably, but a comparatively "obscure" field isn't necessarily going to have the same idea of what progress looks like. The Riemann Hypothesis is making people go "holy shit" because that's been a prestige problem for more than a century. AI has proven tens of thousands of other things in the last few months, but we know to look at this one as the big signifier of progress. If a smaller field doesn't have some widely-known canonical big ticket items, it may be harder to pick up the genuine progress from the dime-a-dozen papers that are correct novel results but aren't particularly interesting.

"Stood on the shoulders of giants" is a cliche for a reason - having a lot of previous work in a field is inherently useful to future advancements, both in terms of knowing how to do things and in terms of knowing which things to do.

children.text: Just like RSA and ECC, AES is based on a fundamentally unproven mathematical conjecture. AES is only "better" in the sense that it is faster and quantum computer resistant. But if one of them gets broken by AI, there is no reason to believe the others are safe. In fact even the post-quantum stuff is not really safe until we actually get some breakthrough mathematical proofs. Our only hope is that P is indeed not equal NP and AI will prove one method's conjecture. Then the entire world can move on to that method and be done with it. Right now it feels like the best you can do is set up a kill switch next to your router.

For (public key) cryptography, there is a chance that factorisation falls to AI before it falls to a quantum computer - I guess it's not impossible that the government can do both already. The question is then whether AI can break "post-quantum" schemes.

For symmetric schemes, I imagine AI will knock off a few bits of security with new techniques, but then we're already at 256 bit keys to have generous reserves. A complete AI break of AES would surprise me.

We are entering a new age where human understanding of things is not important. What is important is proof of things - if we know something to be true it doesn't matter that we understand why, and at some point we will reach a point where we simply can't understand why.

A dog in a car understands the cars ability to move quickly from place to place, but no matter how much you simplify it you can never make that dog understand internal combustion. It's a concept beyond the reasoning ability of the dog.

Where is the limit of human reasoning ability? Many will probably consider that notion itself to be insulting, but we are fundamentally no different biologically to any other animal. We have our limits, and the proofs that our AI systems produce will one day be past them, if not already. Even if not already, the proofs will come in thick and fast and we won't be able to simplify them fast enough to keep up
